questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
questions.problem: If $h(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}),$ find $∇h(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate $∇f(x,y)$ at $(2,1)$ if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =2x\sqrt{y+3} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y+3}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),\,{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\sqrt{y+3},\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y+3}}⟩ \\ ∇f(2,1) & =⟨2\cdot 2\sqrt{1+3},\,\frac{{2}^{2}}{2\sqrt{1+3}}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
questions.problem: Given  $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})$, find $∇g(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot x-\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\cdot 2y \\  & =\frac{1}{y}-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & ={g}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{y}-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}))\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate $∇h(x,y)$ at $(1,1)$ if $h(x,y)=4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y \\ {h}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y) & =⟨{h}_{x}(x,y),\,{h}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡y,\,\frac{4x}{{y}^{2}+1}⟩ \\ ∇h(1,1) & =⟨4\operatorname{arctan}⁡1,\,\frac{4\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{4}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
questions.problem: Given $h(x,y,z)=xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)$, find $∇h(x,y,z).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)) \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}⁡(z) \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)) \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(z) \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)) \\  & =xy\cdot \frac{1}{z} \\  & =\frac{xy}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & ={h}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{h}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{h}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)\text{ }i+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)\text{ }j+\frac{xy}{z}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
questions.problem: Given $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{xyz}$, find $∇f(x,y,z).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xyz}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot (yz) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{xyz}}{2x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xyz}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot (xz) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{xyz}}{2y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xyz}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot (xy) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{xyz}}{2z}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{xyz}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xyz}}{2y}\text{ }j+\frac{\sqrt{xyz}}{2z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{xyz}}{2}(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate $∇f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(2,3,1)$ if $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{xyz}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{xyz})) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot yz \\  & =\frac{1}{2x} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{xyz})) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot xz \\  & =\frac{1}{2y} \\ {f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{xyz})) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{xyz}}\cdot xy \\  & =\frac{1}{2z}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{f}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{2z}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,1) & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 2}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\cdot 3}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{2\cdot 1}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{6}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{2}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find $∇g(x,y,z)$ given that  $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+yz{e}^{xyz} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2{x}^{2}y{z}^{2}+xz{e}^{xyz} \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+{e}^{xyz}) \\  & =2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+xy{e}^{xyz}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,  the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+yz{e}^{xyz})\text{ }i+(2{x}^{2}y{z}^{2}+xz{e}^{xyz})\text{ }j+(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+xy{e}^{xyz})\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find $∇g(x,y,z)$ given that  $g(x,y,z)=\sqrt{x+2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{yz}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x+2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{yz})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+2}}+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+2}} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{yz})) \\  & =0+\frac{1}{\sqrt{yz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{yz}}\cdot z \\  & =\frac{1}{2y} \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x+2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{yz})) \\  & =0+\frac{1}{\sqrt{yz}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{yz}}\cdot y \\  & =\frac{1}{2z}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,  the gradient is:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+2}}i+\frac{1}{2y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{2z}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ find the points $(x,y),$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0 \\ 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2y & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=0,$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$

- For $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0,$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ at two points: $(1,0)$ and $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
questions.problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x,$ find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇g(x,y)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x) \\  & =\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{9}{y}-\frac{3y}{x}+x) \\  & =-\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{3}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇g(x,y)=(\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1)i-(\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{y})j.$

Now, we solve $∇g(x,y)=0:$

$$
(\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1)i-(\frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x})j=0\,i+0\,j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}+1=0 \\ \frac{9}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{{(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})}^{2}}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ 9\cdot {(-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})}^{2}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{81}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{3}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{81+3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}} & =0 \\ 81+3{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =-27 \\ x & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-3,$ we get $y=-\frac{(-3)^{2}}{3}=-3.$

Therefore, $∇g(x,y)=0$ at the point: $(-3,-3).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-x$, find the points $(x,y)$ where $∇f(x,y)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-x) \\  & =6x+0-1 \\  & =6x-1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-x) \\  & =0+2y-0 \\  & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=(6x-1)\,i+2y\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$

$$
(6x-1)\,i+2y\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}6x-1=0 \\ 2y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=\frac{1}{6}.$ From the second equation, we obtain $y=0.$ 

Therefore, $∇f(x,y)=0$ at the point $(\frac{1}{6},0)\,.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z$, find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇f(x,y,z)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}+0-\frac{1}{z{x}^{2}}-0 \\  & =-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}+0-0 \\  & =-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =0+0-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}x}-1 \\  & =-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}=0 \\ -\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=-1.$ Substituting these into the third equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x} & =0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}(-1)}{{z}^{2}(-1)} & =0 \\ 1-{z}^{2} & =0 \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{(-1)^{2}yz} & =0 \\ z+y & =0 \\ y & =-z\end{aligned}
$$

When $z=1,$ we have $y=-1$ and when $z=-1,$ we have $y=1.$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(-1,1,-1).$

questions.problem: Given $h(x,y,z)=xy+x{y}^{2}+{z}^{3}.$ Find the points $(x,y,z)$ where $∇h(x,y,z)=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+x{y}^{2}+{z}^{3}) \\  & =y+{y}^{2}+0 \\  & =y+{y}^{2} \\ {h}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+x{y}^{2}+{z}^{3}) \\  & =x+2xy+0 \\  & =x+2xy \\ {h}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+x{y}^{2}+{z}^{3}) \\  & =0+0+3{z}^{2} \\  & =3{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇h(x,y,z)=(y+{y}^{2})\,i+(x+2xy)\,j+3{z}^{2}\,k.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+{y}^{2})\,i+(x+2xy)\,j+3{z}^{2}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y+{y}^{2}=0 \\ x+2xy=0 \\ 3{z}^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The first equation can be written as $y(1+y)=0$, which gives $y=0$ or $y=-1.$ Substituting these into the second equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2x(0) & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

or,

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2x(-1) & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the third equation, we get $z=0.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(0,0,0)$ and $(0,-1,0).$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
questions.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2},\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=(2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =\frac{1}{xy},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fh]=h\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}((2xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2xy)\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2xy+{y}^{2}}{xy}\text{ }i+\frac{{x}^{2}+2xy}{xy}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}\text{ }i-\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\text{ }j) \\  & =(\frac{2x+y}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{x+2y}{y}\text{ }j)+(-\frac{x+y}{x}\text{ }i-\frac{x+y}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =(-\frac{x+y}{x}+\frac{2x+y}{x})\text{ }i+(-\frac{x+y}{y}+\frac{x+2y}{y})\text{ }j \\  & =\text{ }i+\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
questions.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j) \\  & =y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }j+y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j \\  & =[y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+y\text{ }i]+[x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)\text{ }j+x\text{ }j] \\  & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1)\text{ }i+x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
questions.problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y)$ if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ and $g(x,y)={e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fg]=f∇g+g∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})={y}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})=2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j={y}^{2}\text{ }i+2xy\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})})=-2x{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})})=-2y{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\text{ }j=-2x{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\text{ }i-2y{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =x{y}^{2}(-2x{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\text{ }i-2y{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\text{ }j)+{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}({y}^{2}\text{ }i+2xy\text{ }j) \\  & ={e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}(-2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\text{ }i-2x{y}^{3}\text{ }j)+{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}({y}^{2}\text{ }i+2xy\text{ }j) \\  & ={e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}({y}^{2}(1-2{x}^{2})\text{ }i+2xy(1-{y}^{2})\text{ }j).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $g(x,y)h(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x,y) & =3{x}^{2}-4y,\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=6x\text{ }i-4\text{ }j, &  &  \\ h(x,y) & =2{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\, &  & ∇h(x,y)=4x{y}^{2}\text{ }i+4{x}^{2}y\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $g(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[gh]=h\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,h
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[g(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇g(x,y)+g(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}(6x\text{ }i-4\text{ }j)+(3{x}^{2}-4y)(4x{y}^{2}\text{ }i+4{x}^{2}y\text{ }j) \\  & =(2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot 6x\text{ }i-2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot 4\text{ }j)+((3{x}^{2}-4y)\cdot 4x{y}^{2}\text{ }i+(3{x}^{2}-4y)\cdot 4{x}^{2}y\text{ }j) \\  & =12{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\text{ }i-8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\text{ }j+(12{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-16x{y}^{3})\text{ }i+(12{x}^{4}y-16{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(24{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-16x{y}^{3})\text{ }i+(12{x}^{4}y-24{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\, &  & ∇f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,k, &  &  \\ h(x,y,z) & =\frac{1}{xyz},\, &  & ∇h(x,y,z)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{1}{xy{z}^{2}}\text{ }k. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.
$$

Using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)+f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{1}{xyz}({y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,k)+x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{1}{xy{z}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{xyz}\,i+\frac{2xy{z}^{3}}{xyz}\,j+\frac{3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}{xyz}\,k-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}z}\,j-\frac{x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}}{xy{z}^{2}}\,k \\  & =\frac{y{z}^{2}}{x}\,i+2{z}^{2}\,j+3yz\,k-\frac{y{z}^{2}}{x}\,i-{z}^{2}\,j-yz\,k \\  & ={z}^{2}\,j+2yz\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Two Variables
canonical_examples.problem: Find $\nabla f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,\pi)$ given that $f(x,y) = (x - y)\cos y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y-(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the gradient at the specified point, we substitute $(x,y)= (1,\pi)$ into the above, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(1,\pi ) & ={f}_{x}(1,\pi )\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(1,\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +(1-\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient of a Function of Three Variables
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\nabla g(x,y,z)$   at $(2,-1,3)$ if $g(x,y,z) = x^2 + xyz.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =2x+yz \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =0+xz \\  & =xz \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =0+xy \\  & =xy\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+(xz)\text{ }j+(xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇g(2,-1,3) & =(2(2)+(-1)(3))\text{ }i+2(3)\text{ }j+2(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =1\text{ }i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y-4)\ln (x-2),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\frac{y-4}{x-2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j = 0 \  \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{x-2}=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y-4=0,$ which means $y=4.$  From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x-2)=0,$ which means that $x=3.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf  0$ at the point $(3,4).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y) g(x,y)$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\sqrt{xy},\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by

$$
\nabla [fg] = g \, \nabla\! f  + f \, \nabla\! g.
$$

Using the product rule shown above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+xy(\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }i+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j)+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }i+x\text{ }j).\end{aligned}
$$
